Implementing strategy: Outcome 1: Capacity and Participation • Outcome Statement: Strengthen the capacity of citizens and sub-national administrations to access, understand, and use budget information and digital participatory tools for effective engagement inlocal fiscal decision-making. • Strategic Intervention: The project will build the capacity of citizens and responsive local authorities by combining structured capacity building, institutional strengthening, and digital engagement. This integrated approach simultaneously increases citizen capability, institutional readiness, and access to information. • SILAKA Specific Interventions: Under this outcome, SILAKA leads the demand-side capacity-building work by producing and rolling out standardized local PFM and GRB training packages. These materials are translated into simplified languages to explicitly highlight the social and gender costs of traditional infrastructure over-allocation. SILAKA conducts training for target groups (youth, and Commune Committee representatives) on local budgeting processes, Circular 007 social service allocations, public procurement regulations, and action research methodologies. To operationalize the digital and public engagement goals, SILAKA coordinates awareness campaigns on Citizens Budget, PIDOR, ISAF, and OWSO mobile applications, alongside a dedicated Podcast Series addressing taxation and sub-national budget oversight to build broad public demand. Outcome 2: Accountability and Oversight • Outcome Statement: Strengthen citizen-led monitoring and accountability mechanisms to track public expenditure, promote transparency, and improve government responsiveness. • Strategic Intervention: The project will operationalise accountability by shifting trained citizens from passive participants to active leaders of oversight and advocacy processes through citizen initiatives and activities that generate evidence and engage directly with government platforms. • SILAKA Specific Interventions: SILAKA shifts trained youth and community representatives from passive participants to active monitors of sub-national finances. This is achieved by supporting youth groups to conduct and draft rigorous Gender Analysis Assessments and co-leading Action Research on Local Planning and Budgeting (evaluating CIP formulation, Sangkat fund expenditures, and OWS delivery). SILAKA provides technical support and analysis of the C/S fund to review local procurement processes with social and gender-sensitive specifications. Additionally, SILAKA helps establish offline feedback and assessment documentation channels, allowing citizens to rate local services. These empirical findings are then presented directly to sub-national authorities during joint multi-stakeholder public dialogue forums to drive administrative responsiveness. Outcome 3: Institutionalisation and Sustainability • Outcome Statement: Institutionalise inclusive, transparent, and responsive mechanisms within sub-national administrations for sustained citizen participation. • Strategic Intervention: The project will transition from project-driven engagement to system-level institutionalisation of participatory governance. These interventions ensure that participation-related policies and practices are revised, tested, and implemented to promote effective civic participation in local budget/fiscal management. • SILAKA Specific Interventions: To transition local governance from project-dependent inputs to permanent administrative habits, SILAKA facilitates the Community Development Visioning dialogues, bringing commune/district councilors and citizens together to jointly develop procedures and planning mechanisms. SILAKA leads the technical development and piloting of the standardized Commune/District GRB Checklist to integrate it intoofficial planning protocols. Finally, SILAKA provides direct coaching to commune councilors to draft and validate local civic engagement guidelines and explicit, validated Gender Key Performance Indexes (Gender KPIs), securing NASLA and NCDDS endorsement to embedGRB permanently within sub-national civil service workflows.
DATA → DIALOGUE → DECISION → DELIVERY approach: Stage 1: DATA — Building the Evidence Base through GAA Advocacy is most effective when backed by solid evidence. SILAKA begins by training youth networksand CBOs to conduct a comprehensive Gender Analysis Assessment (GAA). • Methodology: Youth are trained in gender analysis, basic social research, and the requirements of MoI Circular 007. Working with local communities, they map specific, unaddressed gender and social needs in their villages. • Focus Areas: The GAA documents critical service gaps that are often overlooked in standard planning, such as: o Travel barriers and costs preventing pregnant women from accessing health clinics. o Gaps in local, safe vocational training and livelihood programs for young women. o Inadequate child protection, early childhood education, and clean water facilities. • Strategic Value: The GAA produces a structured, localized dataset. This research provides the CCWC and the Commune Council with the evidence-based documentation needed to improve social service expenditures during technical budget reviews with district and provincial authorities.
Stage 2: DIALOGUE — AddressingPower Dynamics via Joint Advocacy A major barrier to local governance reform is the vertical power asymmetry within sub-national administrations. Commune Councils often feel restricted by administrative hierarchies and are hesitant to demand flexible resources from higher-level district or provincial bodies. SILAKA’s dialogue model addresses this issue by establishing a strategic partnership between youth and local councils: • The Youth as Independent Advocates: Because youth groups operate outside theformal government hierarchy, they are not bound by the same bureaucratic constraints as commune councillors. They can raise clear, direct demands for resource reallocation and social spending without fear of administrative pushback. •The Collaboration Strategy: Under SILAKA’s framework, the Commune Council provides youth with the formal entry point and legitimacyto participate in District Integration Workshops. In turn, youth act as an independent voice, presenting GAA data to demand resources and services that the council itself may be unable to lobby for directly. This joint advocacy model shifts the local dynamic froma patron-client relationship to a collaborative, solution-oriented alliance. • Monthly Coordination Platforms: To maintain this partnership, SILAKA integrates youth-led agendas directly into the Commune Council (CC) monthly meetings. This ensures that the CommuneDevelopment Plan (CDP) and Commune Investment Plan (CIP) are updated continuously based on citizen-led evidence.
Stage 3:DECISION — Locking Voice into Budgets via Gender KPIs To ensure that dialogue results in real resource commitments, SILAKA supports the translation of community priorities into formal Gender Indicators (Gender KPIs): • The Technical Process: SILAKA provides direct technical assistance to Commune Councillors (specifically targeting CCWC members) to draft precise, legally auditable budget indicators. • The Mechanism: When citizens identify a critical social gap, that gap is written as a formal, quantified Gender KPI within the commune's official budget guidelines. • The Fiscal Obligation: To secure budget approval, the council is required to commit a specific portion of the C/S Fund directly to that KPI and assign dedicated staff to execute it.
Stage4: DELIVERY — Participatory Procurement and ISAF Integration To ensure that approved funds are spent transparently and result in high-quality services, SILAKA establishes active citizen oversight over the execution phase: • Procurement Monitoring: SILAKA trains youth to monitor local public procurement processes. Participants learn to review bidding announcements, track contractor performance, and verify that materials and services meet agreed-upon specifications. This oversight reduces the risk of collusion and ensures efficient use of the C/S Fund. • Integrationwith the ISAF Process: SILAKA and CLIPS partner pilots these revised civic engagement guidelines and Circular 007 frameworks directly through the formal ISAF (Implementation of the SocialAccountability Framework) response process. By linking the guidelines with the ISAF Joint Action Plans (JAAPs), SILAKA establishes a validated, repeatable operational model. This pilot serves as a concrete blueprint for inclusive local governance that can beintegrated into the national decentralization curriculum.

participating-org.narrative:
SILAKA was incorporated as a non-political, non-sectarian local Cambodian NGO in January 1997 registered with the Ministry of Interior. SILAKA works to identify and provide quality programs and training opportunities for individuals and organizations. Asa leadingcapacity building organization, SILAKA#s offers unsurpassed service and delivery of high quality training and consultant services. SILAKA has the development goal to promote the implementation of democracy in Cambodian society for sustainable development which includes the economic development, including caring for the environment, and social justice.
The Committee to Promote Women in Politics (CPWP) was established in 2005, intended to promote women leaders in public office. The committee ismade of seven local non-government organisations: SILAKA, Gender and Development for Cambodia (GAD/C), Committee for Free and Fair Elections in Cambodia (COMFREL), Neutral and Impartial Committee for Free and Fair Elections in Cambodia (NICFEC), Women forProsperity (WFP), Cambodian Women for Peace and Development (CWPD), and Cambodia Development Research Institute (CDRI). The Coalition for the Promotion of Women in Politics (CPWP) formed in relation to Cambodia#s national and local elections in 2007. Thecoalition was structured under the guidance of international leadership as embodied in the Millennium Developmental Goals. CPWP consists of a colourful mixture of non-government organisations that represent such diverse programs as capacity-building, gender-based initiatives, and research. The timing of the coalition combined with targeted multilateral institutional support in the form of both financial and human resources allocated to the overall effort to galvanise local excitement and opportunity forchange that resulted in the active and genuine participation of the two major project beneficiaries, which are government and the community. Cambodia#s socio-political development over the past two centuries has been wrapped under colonialism and communism, and only recently and in theory has democracy been adopted. What makes CPWP unique to Cambodia is that itis a local nascent coalition based on a participatory and democratic model for action. Just as unique, CPWP is a movement targeting and lead primarily by a traditionally marginalised group, which are women. In some respects, the CPWPmovement can be interpreted as a positive indicator and product of the recent democratic and decentralisation efforts advocated by the international community and implemented by the Cambodian government. CPWP aims to contribute to the creation of a positive and 'empowering'environment for women#s participation in public office. CPWP interventions target local, provincial and national administrators and political partyleaders, potential female candidates and voters as well as the general public. CPWP contributes to the mobilisation of women#s support networks. CPWP envisions a Cambodian society in which women and men enjoy equal access to opportunity and benefits fromsociety. CPWP#s mission statement commits its members to promoting women and men#s equal participation indecision-making and representation in public office; collaborating with each other in developing and implementing joint activities to further theadvancement of women in Cambodian society.
